stt: Steve Jobs' reality distortion takes its toll on truth
x:
The old testament: http://www.amazon.com/Apple-Inside-Macintosh-Volumes-III/dp/...

The new testament: http://www.amazon.com/Inside-Macintosh-Apple-Computer-Inc/dp...

The book of common prayer: http://www.amazon.com/Macintosh-Human-Interface-Guidelines-C...

The dead sea scrolls: http://www.amazon.com/Apple-Reference-Manual-Computers-030-0...

The Apocrypha: http://www.amazon.com/Newton-2-0-User-Interface-Guidelines/d...

Deuterocanonical: http://www.amazon.com/OpenDoc-Programmers-Guide-Apple-Comput...

Dianetics: http://developer.android.com/guide/practices/ui_guidelines/i...

That consistency is phenomenally important for the user.

I had a quick skim, Elementary talk good sense.  It's this apparent trivia that makes the experience.  Like can dialogue text be copied, or how a menu opens, and why.  Or what shortcut keys to use and when.  Or always use the default file open as it'll automatically upgrade visuals and at least some capability when the next OS release comes along. :)

Play along and the user will know how to print, open, copy, preview and a hundred other things on the first ever use of your new program leaving them just to learn the unique new thing.

I kept my Amiga Guidelines phonebook[1] for years after the machine was effectively dead as the principles and explanations were still sound.  The Apple Guidelines[2] were worth owning whether you used a Mac or not, again for the principles, and would often get recommended.  I had a copy years before I ever touched a Mac!  Life got simpler when they were all online.

I don't think it matters where you take cues from, so long as you are internally consistent, and apps carry on that consistency.

[1] http://www.amazon.com/AMIGA-User-Interface-Style-Guide/dp/02...
[2] http://www.amazon.com/Macintosh-Human-Interface-Guidelines-C...

stt: Ask HN: Good books or articles on UI design?
x: The original Macintosh User Interface Guidelines are still worth a read.  Some of them have been forgotten.  A good one is "You should never have to tell the computer something it already knows".

The peak of systematic thinking about UX in tech was arguably the 1984 Macintosh Human Interface Guidelines (https://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/0201622165/guidebook...).

Unfortunately it only took a few years for Apple to start sliding away from their own guidelines, and Windows was always less rigorous to begin with. And then the Web came along and blew the state of UX back to the Stone Age. Sigh.
